Abstract 1

Applied electric fields, the reason behind stray currents, accelerate the ingress of sulfate into cementitious materials. 2

To identify mitigation approaches, this study investigates the effects of slag and fly ash on sodium sulfate attacks of 3

cement pastes under a constant electric current. The mineralogical alterations induced by the attacks were analyzed 4

using X-ray diffractometry, thermogravimetric analysis, scanning electron microscopy, and thermodynamic modeling. 5

The dissolution of aluminates in the slag and fly ash induced a monosulfate-rich area (> ~20 mm from the cathode 6

surface) to form next to the ettringite-rich area on the sample surface (< ~20 mm). This effect reduced the availability 7

of SO42- in the pore solution, thereby hindering the penetration of sulfate. Meanwhile, the consumption of portlandite 8

by the pozzolanic reaction lowered the decalcification resistance of the materials. This produced a wide area that 9

endured the decomposition of portlandite and carbonate-AFm. Overall, blending 30% fly ash did not improve the 10

resistance of the material to either sulfate attacks or decalcification; blending 50% slag can effectively mitigate sulfate 11

ingress, though decalcification may become a governing mechanism in the degradation process. 12

1 Introduction 17

18

Stray current refers to an electric current that flows through buildings, infrastructures, or facilities and is attributable 19

to the imbalance in electric supplies. It can occur whenever voltage differences arise between two objects. Stray- 20

current-induced damage is frequently reported in underground metro tunnels, owing to the wide use of electric 21

traction systems in metro trains. By leaking through tunnel linings into the ground, the stray current can corrode 22

3

reinforcements, debond the steel–concrete interface, and accelerate the penetration of aggressive species into concrete 23

[1-3]. Because of the acceleration of global urbanization, the performance of reinforced concrete subjected to stray 24

currents has become a focus of recent research [4, 5]. 25

26

Sulfate attacks are one of the most recognized degradation mechanisms in underground structures [6, 7]. SO42- from 27

the external environment diffuses into the concrete and reacts with monosulfate, a hydration product of C3A. This 28

reaction leads to the formation of ettringite and subsequent expansion damage [8, 9]. In highly concentrated sulfate- 29

bearing environments, gypsum may also be formed by the reaction between SO42- and portlandite [8, 10]. According 30

to the “crystal growth” theory, expansion is attributable to the crystallization pressure generated by the formation of 31

ettringite under supersaturation conditions at the microscale [10, 11]. At the macro-scale, cracking occurs when the 32

accumulated crystallization pressure surpasses the tensile stress of the cementitious materials [12, 13]. Stray currents 33

are known to accelerate sulfate attacks [14]. This effect can be simulated in the laboratory by applying an electric 34

field to mortar/concrete samples [15, 16]. Previously [17], we investigated sodium and magnesium sulfate attacks of 35

Portland cement pastes under applied electric fields. In contrast to conventional sulfate attacks, we observed a 36

decalcification process and decomposition of ettringite during the late test period. These phase changes were well 37

captured using a thermodynamic modeling approach. 38

39

Supplementary cementitious materials (SCMs) can improve the sulfate resistance of Portland cement-based materials. 40

Physically, most SCMs can refine the material’s pore structure and decelerate the transportation of SO42- [18, 19]. 41

Chemically, SCMs can modify the hydration-phase assemblage in three ways: 1) The pozzolanic reaction of SCMs 42

consumes portlandite and lowers the Ca/Si ratio of C-S-H [20-22]. The formation of gypsum is thus hindered, and 43

supersaturation with respect to ettringite is reduced [18, 19, 23, 24]. It has been reported that the expansion of mortar 44

4

bars blended with SCMs [e.g., silica fume (SF) and ground granulated blast furnace slag (GGBFS)] shows a negative 45

relationship with the Ca/Si ratio of the bulk paste [25]. 2) The C3A in cement can be diluted using SCMs. This effect 46

may reduce expansion, which is typically attributed to monosulfate-ettringite conversion [19, 26]. 3) Certain SCMs 47

such as GGBFS, metakaolin, fly ash (FA), and natural zeolite contain aluminates and have high sulfate binding 48

capacities [27, 28]. Mortars blended with such SCMs usually exhibit smaller early expansion (e.g., < 2 years) [23, 49

29]. However, the total expansion after a longer exposure period can still be significant or even similar to those of 50

plain cement mortars [23, 27]. The use of high-Al slag may exacerbate the sulfate resistance of cementitious materials 51

[29]. 52

53

Blending FA or SF into Portland cement mortar has been reported to decelerate the ingress of sulfate under constant 54

voltages [30, 31]. Because SCMs can refine the pore structure and improve the electric resistance of cementitious 55

materials [32, 33], the improved sulfate resistance in these cases can be attributed to the hindering of the electric 56

current. This effect is a physical aspect of sulfate attacks. Chemically, the influence of SCMs upon the phase 57

alterations of sulfate attacks under applied electric fields remains unknown. Our previous study [17] suggested that 58

decalcification, which occurs simultaneously with sulfate ingress, leads to the decomposition of portlandite, AFm, 59

and C-S-H. Because SCMs consume portlandite via the pozzolanic reaction, it is imperative to test how this effect 60

influences the resistance of materials to decalcification under these circumstances. SCMs are widely used in the 61

manufacture of segmental concrete tunnel liners [34, 35]. Understanding the degradation mechanism of blended 62

cement concrete under applied electric fields will contribute to the design of high-performance tunnel liners resistant 63

against stray currents. Recent studies have indicated that electric fields applied by electrochemical techniques for 64

corrosion protection (e.g., electrochemical rehabilitation and impressed current cathodic protection) may damage the 65

bond between the concrete and reinforcement [36, 37]. Studying the phase alterations of cementitious materials under 66

applied electric fields can also broaden our understanding of the potential risks of these techniques. 67

In this study, a constant electric current was used to simulate the situation when a direct stray current flows through 69

cementitious materials. Sodium sulfate attacks of GGBFS- and FA-blended cement pastes were studied under these 70

conditions. Experimental studies were conducted using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), energy dispersive X- 71

ray spectrometry (EDS), X-ray diffractometry (XRD) with Rietveld refinement, and thermogravimetric analysis 72

(TGA). Thermodynamic modeling was performed to better understand mineralogical alterations and degradation 73

mechanisms. The aim was to address three questions: 1) How do SCMs influence phase alterations when sulfate 74

attacks are induced by electric migration? 2) How do SCMs affect the chemistry of sulfate attacks under a constant 75

electric current? 3) Can decalcification become a leading degradation mechanism of sulfate attack via SCM blending? 76

2.4 Thermodynamic modeling 155

156

The phase assemblage during a diffusion-induced sulfate attack can be simulated by assuming that the hydration 157

products and external sulfate solution mix in various proportions [8-10, 29]. This method is termed “pure 158

thermodynamic modeling” because the transportation equations are neglected. Compared to coupled reactive- 159

transport modeling, pure thermodynamic modeling runs faster; however, the results of both methods are comparable. 160

Under applied electric fields, ionic species migrate in a different manner (Fig. 1); thus, pure thermodynamic modeling 161

cannot be conducted using the same approach. 162

163

Our previous paper [17] demonstrated that electric migration near the surface of a specimen is similar to the scenario 164

in which the ionic species in the pore solution are replaced by those transported from the external solution (Fig. 1b). 165

The sulfate attack near the cathode can be modeled by replacing OH- in the hydrated cement system with SO42- at a 166

mole ratio of OH-:SO42- = 2:1. This method, a “pure thermodynamic modeling” approach, will also be used here to 167

model the effect of SCMs upon phase alterations. 168

169

Geochemical code GEMS 3.3 [40] coupled with the Nagra/PSI [41] and CEMDATA 18 databases (version 18.01) 170

[42] was used for thermodynamic modeling. The CSHQ model was selected, and solid solutions of AFt and AFm 171

were neglected. Siliceous hydrogarnet (C3AS0.8H4.4) and thaumasite were both suppressed, owing to their slow 172

formation kinetics at ambient temperatures [43, 44]. 173

174

Na2SO4 exposure tests were conducted after a hydration period of 28 d; they lasted for an additional 28 d. Therefore, 175

two hydration systems (28 d and 56 d) were modeled for each cementitious system (Table 3). The hydration degrees 176

4.3 Decalcification vs. sulfate attack 449

450

The outflow of the electric current (the cathode side) induces a loss of Ca2+ and hence the decomposition of 451

portlandite, AFm, and C-S-H [17]. In the SCM-blended samples, the portlandite content decreased to a very low level 452

(~2%, Table 6). Moreover, the decomposition of carbonate-AFm became more pronounced. According to 453

thermodynamic modeling, carbonate-AFm has a higher stability than monosulfate under sulfate attacks (Fig. 11c). 454

Thus, we can infer that decalcification is the main factor that destabilizes carbonate-AFm. 455

456

Decalcification, as indicated by the decomposition of carbonate-Afm, influenced a wider area in the FA-blended 457

sample than in the other two samples. Based on the XRD and TG results (Figs. 3 and 4), we may conclude that the 458

resistance of a sample to decalcification negatively correlates with the portlandite content before exposure. This 459

finding differs from our existing understanding: that SCMs can improve calcium leaching resistance in a conventional 460

sulfate attack (in the absence of applied electric fields), by reducing the strength of Ca2+ and OH- in the pore solution 461

[62-64]. One possible reason is the different ionic motion mechanisms under the applied electric fields. Our previous 462

paper [17] suggested that electric current is conveyed by the migration of SO42-, OH-, and Ca2+. Given a constant 463

current, the migrations of different ions influence each other. Once the migration of SO42- is hindered, the migration 464

of Ca2+ and OH- can be enhanced to maintain a stable current. This hypothesis should be tested in future studies. In 465

the SCM-blended samples, decalcification influenced a comparable or even wider area than the sulfate attack (Table 466

6). This suggests that the degradation process can be caused by decalcification rather than sulfate attacks in these 467

samples. 468

4.4 Potential risk of expansion damage 470

471

In this study, we did not measure the expansion of the specimens, owing to the need to apply electric fields via 472

specially designed electrolytic cells. In the existing literature [15, 16, 30, 31], it remains unknown whether sulfate 473

attacks under applied electric fields can induce expansion. In this section, we will analyze whether the potential risk 474

of expansion damage can be mitigated by SCMs, provided that a similar expansion mechanism underlies both 475

diffusion- and migration-induced sulfate attacks. 476

477

One important factor governing the expansion of a sulfate attack is supersaturation with respect to ettringite. SCMs 478

are known to reduce the saturation index of ettringite by (a) restraining the formation of gypsum (because gypsum 479

provides high SO42- strength in the pore solution) [18, 19, 23, 24] and (b) reducing the Ca/Si of the bulk cement paste 480

(which influences the Ca2+ strength in the pore solution) [25]. The SCM-blended samples had a low portlandite 481

content and were subjected to a more pronounced decalcification effect. Referring to mechanism (b), it is likely that 482

GGBFS and FA can reduce the potential risk of expansion damage. 483

484

One remaining question is whether delayed expansion can occur via monosulfate-ettringite conversion, as reported 485

for GGBFS-blended cementitious materials undergoing conventional sulfate attacks [23, 27]. To address this question, 486

we will examine another factor influencing expansion: the confinement of ettringite crystals. In a conventional sulfate 487

attack, SO42- first reacts with large monosulfate crystals deposited in hydrates [11]. The saturation index with respect 488

to ettringite remains low, resulting in almost no expansion. Once the large monosulfate deposits are depleted, the 489

supersaturation of ettringite begins to increase. The monosulfate confined in the mesopores of C-S-H is converted 490

into ettringite, inducing crystallization pressure and expansion damage [11, 29]. For sulfate attacks induced by electric 491

migration, the formation of ettringite starts in the monosulfate-rich area (e.g., areas 15 mm from the cathode). 492

Thermodynamically, large monosulfate deposits (Fig. 7b) are consumed first, resulting in almost no expansion. When 493

these large deposits were depleted, the cement paste became rich in ettringite (e.g., 5 mm from the cathode). The 494

SEM images show that ettringite grew in clusters in the open pores (Fig. 7a). The C-(A-)S-H showed low Ca and S 495

contents relative to their values before the sulfate attack (Table 5). This suggests low Ca2+ and SO42- strengths in the 496

pore solution, which may not support monosulfate-ettringite conversion inside C-(A-)S-H. At a later stage of the 497

sulfate attack, the materials exhibited a porous microstructure owing to the loss of Ca2+ (Fig. 6). Ettringite crystals 498

grew in open pores without confinement; thus, they may be non-expansive. 499

4.5 Designing high-performance cementitious materials resistant against stray currents 501

502

This paper simulates the effect of stray currents by applying electric fields (constant current) to cement paste samples. 503

One important factor governing the degradation mechanism under this circumstance is the ionic motion induced by 504

electric migration. In contrast to a conventional sulfate attack, in which the ionic motion is primarily induced by a 505

concentration gradient (i.e., diffusion), the cations and anions migrate in opposite directions under applied electric 506

fields (Fig. 12a). Simultaneously with the SO42- ingress, decalcification and neutralization can occur owing to the 507

migration of Ca2+ and OH-, respectively [17]. SCM blending can mitigate the ingress of SO42- by releasing aluminates 508

and facilitating monosulfate formation (Section 4.2). It also reduces the portlandite content and bulk Ca/Si ratio of 509

the hydrates, which mitigates potential expansion damage (Section 4.4) but produces a more pronounced 510

decalcification (Section 4.3). Figure 12b illustrates how sulfate ingress and decalcification correlate with the chemical 511

composition and reactivity of the SCMs studied. To design high-performance cementitious materials resistant against 512

5 Conclusions 559

560

This study investigated the chemical effects of direct stray currents, by applying a constant electric current to cement 561

paste specimens. The following conclusions were drawn. 562

563

1) Sulfate attacks occur when electric current flows out of the cementitious materials. In the cement paste sample 564

with 50% GGBFS blending or 30% FA blending, the hydration phase assemblage near the cathode was 565

characterized by the formation of ettringite (0.5–5 mm) and monosulfate (0.5–30/40 mm), and the decomposition 566

of portlandite, carbonate-AFm, and hydrotalcite after 28 days’ exposure to Na2SO4 solutions. 567

568

2) The presence of SCMs favors the reaction of external sulfates with dissolved aluminates to form monosulfates. 569

Such an effect mitigated the formation of ettringite, reduced the availability of SO42- in the pore solution [as 570

suggested by the S content in C-(A-)S-H], and slowed the electric migration of SO42-. Thus, the blended cement 571

paste with 50% GGBFS showed a higher chemical resistance to sulfate attacks than Portland cement paste. In 572

contrast, blending 30% FA did not effectively mitigate sulfate ingress because of the lower reactive aluminate 573

content combined with slower dissolution kinetics. 574

3) Decalcification occurs owing to the outflow of electric current, creating a porous area near the sample surface 576

(0–0.5 mm) and reducing the Ca/Si ratio of C-(A-)S-H in the ettringite-rich area. These effects can mitigate the 577

potential risk of expansion damage. However, the consumption of portlandite by the pozzolanic reaction lowers 578

the resistance of the material against decalcification. The decomposition of carbonate-AFm, a result of 579

decalcification, influenced a wider area than the penetration of sulfate. Thus, in the SCM-blended samples, 580

decalcification may form the leading degradation mechanism in sulfate attacks. 581

582

For future work, potential topics of interest include phase alterations under alternative stray currents, degradation 583

processes influenced by aggregates, etc. Researches in these areas can better bridge the findings of this paper with 584

sulfate attacks in real-world scenarios. 585
